opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rebecca. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won't be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine. I've got forty minutes before a client call, so let's be efficient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've adopted the tools responsibly and clients get faster work at the same quality. That's the firm line, and it's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this world, the billable hour bends but doesn't break. We charge a bit differently, maybe fixed fees for routine deals. I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push the firm to move more work to fixed fees before clients force us to. Keep my client relationships tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Mostly a pricing problem.

S0.say: We've adopted the tools responsibly, and clients get faster work at the same quality.
S0.think: The billable hour bends but doesn't break. It's mostly a pricing problem.
S0.do: Pushes the firm towards fixed fees before clients demand it and keeps her client relationships tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the profession has to think hard about how it trains the next generation. That's a real issue, and I'd say it on panels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We already halved the junior intake. In ten years we'll have too few senior associates, because we didn't train them. That's a firm problem. My own seat is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your seat's safe. Is that the same in private as in public?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in this one. Clients hire me, not the firm's software. Ask me again for the fast version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Argue at the partners' meeting to keep a small, well-trained junior group, even if it costs us now. Mentor two of them myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mildly annoyed at my partners' short-term thinking.

S1.say: The profession has to think hard about how it trains the next generation.
S1.think: Halving junior intake leaves a gap in senior associates later. That's a firm problem, but her own seat is safe.
S1.do: Argues for a small, well-trained junior group and mentors two juniors herself.
S1.feel: Mildly annoyed at her partners' short-term thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI frees lawyers to focus on judgement and strategy. And I'd say the layoffs are hitting women and younger staff hardest, which should worry all of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our paralegals and junior associates are mostly routine work. That's a third of the building. Revenue per partner might even go up for a while, which is grim but true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help plan the cuts, fairly and with decent payouts, because if I don't someone worse will. Put more time into the advisory work clients pay a premium for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. I don't like what I'll be signing.

S2.say: AI frees lawyers to focus on judgement. And the layoffs hit women and younger staff hardest, which should worry us all.
S2.think: A third of the firm does routine work. Profit per partner may even rise for a while, which she finds grim.
S2.do: Helps plan the cuts with decent payouts and puts more time into premium advisory work.
S2.feel: Uncomfortable about what she'll be signing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly, I'd say trusted advisers matter more than ever when things are this uncertain. Clients want a person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your public line is about trusted advisers. Your private one is that the firm doesn't survive. Is that gap hard to hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It's my job to hold it. You don't tell clients the building's on fire while you're still deciding which exit to use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if AI matches a skilled lawyer, the billable hour is dead and the firm shrinks to a handful of partners who hold the clients. I'd probably be one of them. Probably. The firm as I know it doesn't survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lock in my top clients personally. Talk to my husband about what we'd do if the partnership broke up, though money isn't the issue. Back candidates who want the gains taxed properly, because I think they should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. More about losing what I built than money.

S3.say: Trusted advisers matter more than ever when things are this uncertain.
S3.think: The billable hour dies and the firm shrinks to a few partners. She'd probably be one, but the firm she built doesn't survive.
S3.do: Locks in her top clients, talks through a break-up of the partnership with her husband and backs candidates who want gains taxed.
S3.feel: Tense, about losing what she built more than money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is now a question for the whole society, not one profession. I'd be arguing for a proper safety net, funded by those who are gaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much changes from the last one. What changes is my kids. Both still at school, and I can't name a career I'd tell them is safe. That's new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put money aside in trusts for the children. Stop pushing them towards law. Ask them what they actually enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For myself, steady. For my kids, worried.

S4.say: This is a question for the whole society now. Fund a proper safety net from those who are gaining.
S4.think: Little changes for her, but she can't name a career she'd tell her children is safe.
S4.do: Sets up trusts for the children, stops steering them to law and asks what they enjoy.
S4.feel: Steady for herself, worried for her kids.
